headlines.title: 49ers fans head to Australia for season opener with surprise sendoff from Steve Young
headlines.description: Dozens of San Francisco 49ers fans boarded a flight at San Francisco International Airport heading to Melbourne, Australia, to cheer on the team in Thursday’s season opener against the Los Angeles Rams. Before departing on their 16-hour United Airlines flight, travelers were given a surprise sendoff by 49ers legend and Hall of Fame quarterback Steve Young, who wished them safe travels and shook hands with fans at the gate. “Niners fans always travel … just always is,” Young said. The unexpected appearance by one of the franchise’s greatest players set an enthusiastic tone for fans heading down under. “I never met him before … great way to start it off,” said Francisco Vera, a fan from San Jose who is traveling with his wife to celebrate their anniversary. Dwight Hall of Antioch shared a similar sentiment about meeting the former quarterback before boarding. “I felt great, this is once in a lifetime … honor to meet him and see him,” Hall said. The traveling fans will arrive in Australia a couple of days before kickoff, giving many of them time to take in sights around Melbourne before the 49ers face the Rams on Thursday.

headlines.title: Artists demand answers after murals painted over in San Francisco's Clarion Alley
headlines.description: A new fight to preserve a well-known Mission District landmark is underway after several murals were painted over in an alley between 17th and 18th streets and Mission and Valencia streets. Clarion Alley is known for the dozens of murals that fill the space. But the Clarion Alley Mural Project (CAMP) says it is heartbroken and furious after someone painted over several of those public art pieces on Aug. 24. “When something like that happens, it’s like really painful because you know the amount of hours it’s spent to design the mural,” said Nyia Luna, an artist with Graffiti Camp for Girls. Three murals were painted over with white paint, and a fourth was partially destroyed, prompting artists to demand answers and restitution. One of the destroyed works was painted this year by Luna and Graffiti Camp for Girls, a nonprofit that teaches young girls to create public art. After learning what happened, Luna spent more than six hours and about $100 to create a new piece. “It’s a community space, you know, people from around here, locals and then people from across the globe come here to see these murals,” Luna said. Witness and artist Doug Rhodes said he spotted a man rolling white paint over the art and confronted him. “I saw some guy rolling over the murals with white paint with a roller, and I told him to stop, and he said, ‘Oh, my boss told me to do this,'” Rhodes said. Rhodes eventually got the worker to stop. “It’s always infuriating when art gets destroyed out of ignorance,” Rhodes said. “That’s my reaction, like, come on guys, do some due diligence here. Don’t just paint over it.” CAMP representatives said they received no warning before the incident. In an email exchange, Makras Real Estate Group—the realty company associated with the property—said the property owner received a call regarding graffiti and sent a team to remove it. Makras stated they were unaware of the incident until CAMP alerted them. Ivy Jeanne, co-director of the Clarion Alley Mural Project, said the organization is looking into its options to help protect the art moving forward. “This project has been around since 1992, and we have built relationships over these decades with various landlords to paint murals,” Jeanne said. “So it’s very well established that there’s a mural project, and it’s known that that wasn’t graffiti.” Jeanne added that the project hopes to maintain its mission despite the setback. “There’s been over 900 murals, and they have a lot to do with social justice, equity, and so that’s what we hope,” Jeanne said. “We hope to continue to flourish as a project.” For people who work nearby, the loss extends beyond the physical paint on the walls. “A lot of the history of like activism and, you know, again just like having diversity,” said local worker Imani Outen. “I feel like just having those values kind of like painted over or just washed away is just, you know, kind of unfortunate and just disempowering to like the legacy that’s been built for what it’s known for.” Prior to the incident, CAMP had already launched a $35,000 fundraising campaign to mark its upcoming 35th year and support its ongoing efforts in the community.

headlines.title: 2 armed robbery suspects arrested near San Jose scene
headlines.description: Police safely arrested two armed robbery suspects at a nearby apartment complex on Monday afternoon with the help of specialized units, authorities said. Officers responded at approximately 12:06 p.m. to the 1300 block of West San Carlos Street following reports of an armed robbery, according to the San Jose Police Department. According to police, two suspects — one reportedly armed with a firearm and the other with a knife —allegedly stole personal property from a victim. Officers located the suspects shortly after at a neighboring apartment complex, where they were taken into custody without incident with assistance from the department’s Special Operations Unit. No injuries were reported. The case remains an active and ongoing investigation.

headlines.title: 5 injured after scaffolding collapse at Summit Skywalker Ranch
headlines.description: Five men were injured, one seriously, after scaffolding and display screens collapsed during event setup at Summit Skywalker Ranch on Monday morning, emergency officials said. Fire crews responded at 11:23 a.m. to the property, located at 3838 Lucas Valley Road, after an initial dispatch reported three people trapped under a stage. The site was being prepared for an event when scaffolding and display screens collapsed in the upper campus area for unknown reasons. Three of the five injured men were transported to local hospitals. The most severely injured patient suffered a head injury and was transported “code three”—a response considered “very serious,” according to a battalion chief with information related to the accident. One patient became trapped under LCD screens, prompting firefighters to deploy airbags to lift the collapsed structure. That individual was treated at the scene and released. Multiple agencies responded to the incident, including teams from Marin County Fire, the San Rafael Fire Department and the Novato Fire Department. Sheriff’s deputies did not respond to the scene. All fire department units cleared the area by 1:31 p.m. The cause of the collapse remains under investigation by the California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA). The facility, formerly known as Big Rock Ranch, is distinct from the principal Skywalker Ranch property.

headlines.title: Sea lion dies at San Francisco beach amid surge in toxic algal bloom cases
headlines.description: A California sea lion died at San Francisco’s Crissy Field on Monday after showing signs of domoic acid poisoning, according to The Marine Mammal Center in Sausalito. Callers first reported the large sea lion on the beach showing signs of distress, including head weaving and seizures, about 8 a.m. A trained responder from the marine mammal center was dispatched to assess the animal and manage the scene at Crissy Field, a public waterfront area east of the Golden Gate Bridge. While the center was organizing a rescue team, however, the sea lion unfortunately died on the beach, a center spokesperson said. Samples were taken to determine if the animal was suffering from domoic acid poisoning, but the results won’t be available on Monday, according to the center. The Marine Mammal Center has seen a flare-up of sea lions stranding with signs of domoic acid poisonings this year, primarily California sea lions. Domoic acid is produced during certain harmful algal bloom events. The neurotoxin accumulates in small fish, like sardines and anchovies, which are then eaten by marine mammals like sea lions in large quantities. Since Aug. 24, about 40 sea lions have been rescued in Monterey County and southern Santa Cruz County, with additional rescues in San Mateo, San Francisco, Marin and Sonoma counties. A handful of northern fur seals have also been affected. The center said it has already passed its average annual number of domoic acid rescues — normally about 75-90 animals per year across a 600-mile California response range. “As we are currently seeing intense surges of domoic acid along the California coast, our hotline is inundated with reports of animals in need to the tune of 3-6x our normal call volume, with some days seeing nearly 700 calls,” the center said in a statement. In sea lions, the brain is attacked by domoic acid, causing seizures and heart failure. When it’s untreated, it usually causes permanent brain damage, according to the marine mammal center. The toxin will naturally flush from an animal’s system over time, but sea lions repeatedly exposed to the toxin will suffer longer-lasting and more serious effects. Domoic acid also affects humans who eat contaminated crab, shellfish and fish, causing a life-threatening condition known as amnesiac shellfish poisoning, the marine mammal center said. People and their pets should keep their distance from stranded or distressed marine mammals and call the center’s hotline, if they are located between Mendocino and San Luis Obispo County, at 415-289-SEAL (7325). More information is available at https://www.marinemammalcenter.org/ .

headlines.title: Family wants plaques at Vallejo pedestrian bridge to honor Pearl Pinson
headlines.description: Vallejo city councilmembers will consider a plan for two plaques to honor Pearl Pinson, a 15-year-old kidnapped more than 10 years ago while she was on her way to school. The plaques would be installed on each side of a pedestrian bridge investigators believe the teen was dragged over before being stuffed in the trunk of her abductor’s car. “Please approve these plaques even if we have to pay for them,” said Rose Pinson, Pearl’s sister. “To have these plaques approved would not only mean a lot to our family, to our friends, but would mean a lot to the community because it not only tells her story of who she was, it helps prevent another child, another family from going through what we have to go through.” The prime suspect in Pearl Pinson’s kidnapping in the case was shot and killed by police in Solvang a day after the abduction. Pearl Pinson has still not been found. “It’s 10 years,” said James Pinson, Pearl’s father. “It’s like a nightmare you never wake up from.” The family said they gather at the pedestrian bridge every May 25, the day Pearl Pinson was abducted, and on her birthday. The Vallejo City Council will vote on installing the plaques at Tuesday’s meeting. Vallejo May 26 May 25, 2019 Family Holds Vigil for Missing Vallejo Teen

headlines.title: ‘You Can See Everything': New film follows Elizabeth Holmes weeks before prison
headlines.description: A new documentary involving former Theranos CEO and convicted felon Elizabeth Holmes has left Silicon Valley buzzing and stunned. “You Can See Everything” is a documentary about the final weeks before Holmes went to prison. In fact, she invited a documentary crew into her home to follow her and her family around. People are now wondering why Holmes would invite a film crew after being found guilty of fraud and sentenced to more than a decade in prison. “I think it’s going to give us a window into the makeup of some people who fit the profile of Elizabeth Holmes, superstars from a very young age,” said Aron Solomon, chief strategy officer for Amplify. “Look at all the 30 under 30 people since Elizabeth Holmes that have been charged with crimes. I think it’s going to give us some insight into their psychological makeup, with Elizabeth Holmes as an exemplar.” A24, who produced the film, is set to release the documentary in theaters in October. Holmes went to prison in Texas in 2023. She was sentenced originally to more than 11 years, but ended up with 10 years and three months. headlines.title: Bay Area firefighters traveling to New York City for 9/11
headlines.description: Firefighters from the Bay Area are traveling to New York City to honor the lives lost on 9/11 25 years ago. The first responders also want to honor the hundreds of firefighters who have died since then from toxic dust and other illnesses contracted at Ground Zero. Janelle Wang has more, including a closer look at a Bay Area honor guard, in the video above. headlines.title: Warming trend sparks heat advisory for Bay Area and Central Coast
headlines.description: A heat advisory will be in effect for the Bay Area by midweek when rising temperatures are expected to peak. The National Weather Service said the heat advisory will start 10 am. Wednesday through 10 p.m. Thursday for the Bay Area and Central Coast. Temperatures are expected to range from 90-105 degrees in the interior, with the coast seeing mid-70s to low-90s. Get your full Microclimate Forecast at nbcbayarea.com/weather. headlines.title: 2 people stabbed following dispute in Sunnyvale
headlines.description: Police are investigating after two people were stabbed following a dispute in Sunnyvale late Sunday night. The stabbing was reported at about 11:33 p.m. in the area of 756 San Juan Drive, according to the Sunnyvale Department of Public Safety. Authorities said the two victims were involved in a dispute with a suspect that escalated into an altercation. Both victims were stabbed multiple times before taking off from the scene. The victims called 911 and were taken to a local hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening. The case remains under investigation, authorities said.

headlines.title: Highway 101 reopens in San Francisco after Labor Day weekend closures
headlines.description: Highway 101 through San Francisco reopened Monday morning following three days of closures for repaving work. The northbound lanes had been closed as Caltrans crews worked to restore the highway surface, forcing Labor Day weekend drivers to use alternate routes around the work zones. The project included repaving the highway and replacing rebar beneath the new asphalt. A Caltrans spokesperson said Sunday night that crews were waiting for newly poured concrete to cure and harden enough to withstand the weight of traffic. Caltrans said the work was scheduled for the holiday weekend because traffic volumes are typically lower along that stretch of highway during the long weekend. The agency is expected to provide an update Monday morning on the project and additional closures planned for more work along the same stretch of Highway 101 in two weeks.

headlines.title: Authorities investigate another possible mountain lion sighting in San Francisco
headlines.description: A mountain lion sighting near Fell and Baker Saturday night prompted a big response. On Sunday, Animal Care and Control said the threat appears to be over; however, authorities said there was an unconfirmed mountain lion sighting on Sunday. Peter Tira with the California Department of Fish and Wildlife says they were among those called in on Saturday, but never actually saw a mountain lion. They monitored the tree and checked back again Sunday morning. Tira says it does not mean there was not a lion, as one was spotted in the Pac Heights area in January, captured and released back into the wild. “They typically come from the coast, from the Peninsula where there is a good population of lions and they can move up through the Peninsula up into wild habit, the wilder natural habitat, if you look at the map, the Panhandle is kind of connected to Golden Gate Park,” Tira said. He says it’s impossible to say where it went but the panhandle is connected to a lot of habitats leading all the way to the coast. So, the best-case scenario is that it follows the same path back. On Sunday, Animal Care and Control said there’s no longer a threat and it is believed the animal left the area. Hours later, authorities said someone reported a mountain lion sighting in the area of 44th and Fulton at 3 p.m.
